extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent applicants, and practitioners preparing or prosecuting U.S. patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the USPTO duty of candor and disclosure for U.S. nonprovisional patent applications, including who owes the duty, what must be disclosed, how to disclose (IDS), timing windows, and fee consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor and good faith / duty of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO imposes a duty of candor and good faith in dealing with the USPTO upon each individual associated with the filing and prosecution of a patent application. The duty of candor and good faith includes a duty to disclose to the USPTO all information material to patentability known to each said individual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an affirmative duty to provide material information to assure good faith in proceedings with the USPTO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who owes the duty of disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of disclosure falls on everyone associated with the preparation, filing, or prosecution of a patent application. This includes: each inventor named in the application, each attorney or agent who prepares or prosecutes the application, and every other person (i) who is substantively involved in the preparation or prosecution of the application and (ii) who is associated with the inventor, the applicant, an assignee, or anyone to whom there is an obligation to assign the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-prong test for 'every other person': (i) substantive involvement in preparation/prosecution and (ii) association with inventor/applicant/assignee/obligated assignee.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to satisfy the duty: file an IDS
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of disclosure is accomplished by submitting an Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) containing the material information to the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File an IDS form listing material information; the duty continues throughout the life of the patent application and new information discovered should be disclosed in a timely manner (e.g., cited in a related or foreign counterpart application).

rubrics_metrics.name: What is an IDS
rubrics_metrics.description: An Information Disclosure Statement (IDS) is a form filed with the USPTO in a U.S. patent application listing information that may be material to the patentability of the subject application (i.e., relevant information) that is known to individuals associated with that patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the IDS form to identify patents, applications, publications, products, etc., that may be material. Discuss timing and strategy with counsel as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability: only U.S. nonprovisional applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The duty of disclosure only exists for U.S. nonprovisional patent applications, i.e., utility, design, and plant patent applications. Thus, an IDS only needs to be filed in a U.S. nonprovisional patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An IDS may not be filed in a U.S. provisional patent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search obligation (no affirmative search required)
rubrics_metrics.description: No searching is necessary; however, if a search has been performed, the relevant references found in the search must be disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performing a search creates an obligation to disclose references found by that search. Not performing a search does not relieve the duty to disclose known material information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compulsory disclosure and sanctions for failure
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosure of relevant information is compulsory in order for a patent application to proceed to grant; failure to disclose all known information material to patentability may result in refusal to grant a patent or cancellation of a granted patent for violation of the duty of disclosure through bad faith or intentional misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclose known material information to avoid sanctions; consult counsel about borderline items. Note: disclosing information to the USPTO is not construed to be an admission that the information is, or is considered to be, material to patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition / threshold: 'material to patentability'
rubrics_metrics.description: Information that is 'material to patentability' should be disclosed. Information is 'material to patentability' if it is relevant to the invention claimed in your patent application; that is if the information establishes a prima facie case of patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of potentially material information include patents, patent applications, patent application publications, products, and any other publication (e.g., articles, research papers, videos, books, products, etc.) relevant to the claimed invention. (Use caution: consult counsel on borderline relevance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: When to disclose patents and published patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reference is a patent or published patent application, it will need to be disclosed if the filing date of the patent or published application predates the filing date or priority date of your patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare filing/publication dates against your application's filing or priority date to determine disclosure obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to disclose non-patent literature (NPL)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the reference is non-patent literature (books, articles, products, etc.), it should be disclosed if the first date the item was published, offered for sale, used, or known predates the filing date or priority date of your patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish the earliest date of public availability/offer/use/knowledge to determine whether the NPL predates your filing/priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple IDS filings permitted and common
rubrics_metrics.description: You can file more than one IDS in a single patent application, and it is common to file more than one IDS throughout the prosecution of a U.S. patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are several reasons to file more than one IDS; discuss timing and strategy with your patent attorney.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government fee for filing an IDS
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes a government fee must be paid when filing an IDS, but it depends on when the IDS is filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The government fee ranges from $52 to $260, depending on the entity status of the patent applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended timing windows to avoid an IDS fee
rubrics_metrics.description: It's best to meet the duty of disclosure within one of the following windows to avoid a government fee: within three (3) months of filing an application; within three (3) months of when new information is made known to an individual associated with the patent application; within three (3) months of when the information was cited in a counterpart foreign patent application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing within these windows generally avoids fees; file as soon as practicable because the USPTO's timing of the first Office Action is unpredictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Late disclosure and fee exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is possible to disclose information after these time periods with the payment of a USPTO fee. However, if you file an IDS after three months from the application filing date but before a first Office Action, no fee is due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because you never know when the USPTO will issue the first Office Action, the sooner an IDS is filed, the better. If disclosing late, expect potential fees and consult counsel regarding fee calculations and timing.
